review.research_question: How are AI interviewers designed and evaluated, and how do they affect interview quality, respondent experience, and resulting data compared with human or conventional interviewing?

writing_instructions: Organize the report by themes and claims, not by paper.
Treat claim statements as bounded synthesis propositions, not immutable conclusions.
Weight evidence using appraisal and applicability; do not count findings as equal votes.
Represent supporting, contradicting, and qualifying evidence fairly.
Preserve source locators for every substantive empirical statement.
Do not infer that unused or unavailable evidence is negative evidence.

themes.label: Disclosure, trust, and evaluation apprehension
themes.description: How perceived automation, social judgment, familiarity, and trust shape willingness to disclose; excludes claims about the truth or validity of disclosed content.

themes.label: Adaptive probing and conversational quality
themes.description: How probe type, timing, listening behavior, rapport, and autonomy affect response production and interview quality.

themes.label: Respondent burden and deployment trade-offs
themes.description: Time, attrition, usability, acceptability, and the practical costs of conversational data collection.

themes.label: Measurement validity and evidential value
themes.description: Whether AI-collected or AI-coded material is correct, novel, construct-valid, and useful for inference, distinct from verbosity or engagement.

claims.statement: AI interviewers can approach trained-human transcript quality under constrained online conditions, but autonomy and modality alter rapport and performance enough to preclude a general equivalence claim.
claims.scope: Short online or embodied interviews evaluated through transcript ratings and post-interview experience.

evidence.rationale: Blinded sociology evaluators rated AI voice competitively with human face-to-face interviews under specified benchmarks.

finding.author_claim: Short AI-led interviews approached or exceeded trained-human interview quality under matched online constraints, especially with voice input.
finding.evidence_statement: Against an online-text expert benchmark, mean grades were 3.93 for AI voice, 3.51 for human face-to-face, 2.98 for AI text, and 2.42 for human text; against a face-to-face benchmark they were 3.50, 3.53, 2.70, and 1.99 respectively, with 40 ratings per modality.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Blinded expert ratings support competitive transcript quality, but small modality cells, heterogeneous topics, and subjective benchmarks limit claims of equivalence.
finding.direction: AI voice comparable; AI text mixed
finding.measure: sociology PhD ratings relative to hypothetical expert benchmarks

study.label: Geiecke and Jaravel matched modality expert evaluation
study.design: multi-modality comparative evaluation with blinded transcript graders
study.population: behavioral-lab interview respondents across five qualitative topics
study.setting: 30-minute face-to-face, online text, or online voice interviews
study.intervention: GPT-4o AI interviewer using text or voice
study.comparator: trained human experts interviewing face-to-face or by online text chat
methods: eight sociology PhD transcript evaluators blinded to transcript modality
measures: quality relative to hypothetical expert text-chat interview
quality relative to hypothetical expert face-to-face interview

appraisal.framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal

dimensions.name: internal validity
dimensions.rationale: Graders were blinded to modality, but the small modality samples and differences in input mode and topic complicate causal attribution.

dimensions.name: measurement validity
dimensions.rationale: Expert transcript ratings are directly relevant but subjective and benchmark a hypothetical expert.

dimensions.name: external validity
dimensions.rationale: Multiple topics help, but interviews were short and conducted in constrained behavioral-lab or online settings.

appraisal.applicability: Direct comparison of AI and trained-human qualitative interview transcripts under online constraints.

sources.title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews
sources.author: Geiecke, Friedrich and Jaravel, Xavier

evidence.rationale: Fully automatic SimSensei underperformed its Wizard-of-Oz predecessor on listening, usability, and rapport.

finding.author_claim: Automation still lagged the Wizard-of-Oz system on important interaction-quality measures.
finding.evidence_statement: The automatic system scored lower for being a good listener (3.56 vs 4.10, d=0.61), system usability (68.68 vs 74.37, d=0.44), and rapport (75.43 vs 80.71, d=0.44), with differences marked p<.05.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: A system can sustain interviews while still losing meaningful conversational quality when human control is removed.
finding.measure: post-interview listener item, System Usability Scale, and rapport measure

study.label: SimSensei automatic-versus-Wizard-of-Oz evaluation
study.design: comparative user study across separately recruited system cohorts
study.population: adult volunteers recruited through Craigslist and flyers
study.setting: 15-25 minute semi-structured health interview with the Ellie virtual human
methods: comparison of 91 automatic-system interviews with 140 Wizard-of-Oz interviews

appraisal.framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal

dimensions.name: internal validity
dimensions.rationale: The automatic and Wizard-of-Oz samples were separately recruited cohorts rather than randomized concurrent conditions.

dimensions.name: measurement validity
dimensions.rationale: Established usability and rapport measures complement direct sharing items, but the evidence is predominantly post-interview self-report.

dimensions.name: external validity
dimensions.rationale: Volunteer recruitment and a single health-interview prototype constrain population and platform generalization.

appraisal.overall_judgment: low confidence for causal effects; moderate confidence for feasibility
appraisal.applicability: Directly relevant to embodied automated health interviewers and system-design tradeoffs.

sources.title: SimSensei Kiosk: A Virtual Human Interviewer for Healthcare Decision Support
sources.author: DeVault, David and Artstein, Ron and Benn, Grace and Dey, Teresa and Fast, Ed and Gainer, Alesia and Georgila, Kallirroi and Gratch, Jonathan and Hartholt, Arno and Lhommet, Margaux and others

evidence.rationale: Willingness to share was retained even as interaction-quality measures declined.

finding.author_claim: The fully automatic system retained the prototype's ability to support personal sharing.
finding.evidence_statement: Automatic and Wizard-of-Oz cohorts were similar on willingness to share (4.07 vs 4.03), comfort sharing (3.80 vs 3.92), and feeling good talking (3.60 vs 3.69); reported differences were small and not marked significant.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Feasibility is supported, but the nonrandomized cross-cohort comparison does not establish equivalence or causal effects on disclosure.
finding.measure: post-interview Likert items

evidence.rationale: Full-text evidence added in the expanded reviewed tranche.

finding.author_claim: AI interviews can sustain effort and reveal explanations hidden beneath one-shot answers.
finding.evidence_statement: More than 95% completed the interview; the median interview lasted 27 minutes and produced about 610 respondent words, while probing revealed risk beliefs and investing misconceptions obscured by initial low-income explanations.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: This is strong feasibility and discovery evidence, although the value of emergent themes is not equivalent to criterion validity.
finding.measure: completion, duration, text volume, and inductive themes

evidence.rationale: Full-text evidence added in the expanded reviewed tranche.

finding.author_claim: Chatbot collection did not provide a general longitudinal data-quality or experience advantage.
finding.evidence_statement: Web surveys often had more favorable response characteristics and quality, chatbot respondents supplied fewer words over time, and chatbot ratings of enjoyment, usefulness, and security were lower, although attention-check performance favored the chatbot.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Conversational interfaces can underperform conventional forms when repeated use and privacy perceptions matter; effects depend on metric and deployment horizon.
finding.measure: response behavior, attention checks, and user ratings

dimensions.rationale: Conversational interfaces can underperform conventional forms when repeated use and privacy perceptions matter; effects depend on metric and deployment horizon.

sources.title: Comparing Chatbots and Online Surveys for (Longitudinal) Data Collection: An Investigation of Response Characteristics, Data Quality, and User Evaluation
sources.author: Zarouali, Brahim and Araujo, Theo and Ohme, Jakob and de Vreese, Claes

evidence.rationale: Full-text evidence added in the expanded reviewed tranche.

finding.author_claim: The conversational survey increased engagement and response quality.
finding.evidence_statement: The chatbot elicited 39% more information and 25.7% higher aggregate response quality across informativeness, relevance, specificity, and clarity than the conventional survey.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: A bounded pre-LLM adaptive system can improve coded open-response quality at scale, though Gricean metrics do not establish broader validity.
finding.measure: human-coded Gricean response quality

sources.author: Xiao, Ziang and Zhou, Michelle X. and Liao, Q. Vera and Mark, Gloria and Chi, Changyan and Chen, Wenxi and Yang, Huahai

evidence.rationale: Full-text evidence added in the expanded reviewed tranche.

finding.author_claim: AI and human text interviews showed different pacing but similar coded specificity and relevance.
finding.evidence_statement: Humans elicited longer responses per question, while the AI asked questions faster and produced longer interviews overall; coded specificity and relevance did not differ significantly.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Holding text modality constant narrows the comparison, but the small sample and non-expert human benchmark preclude an equivalence conclusion.
finding.measure: response length and coded specificity and relevance

finding.author_claim: Active-listening capabilities improved engagement and elicited response quality.
finding.evidence_statement: The full chatbot significantly outperformed the baseline across agent comprehension, user interest, chat experience, engagement duration, response word count, and manually coded response quality.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Specific conversational capabilities—not chatbot presence alone—can improve elicitation, although intent models performed unevenly across topics.
finding.measure: user ratings, engagement, word count, and coded response quality

finding.author_claim: Dividing topics across managed agents improved elicitation and conversational flow.
finding.evidence_statement: CommunityBots participants were significantly more engaged, provided more specific, clear, and expansive responses, and experienced fewer conversational interruptions than the single-agent baseline.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Interviewer architecture and topic management affect output, but the multi-agent treatment bundles several interface and conversation changes.
finding.measure: engagement, coded quality, and interruptions

sources.author: Jiang, Zhiqiu and Rashik, Mashrur and Panchal, Kunjal and Jasim, Mahmood and Sarvghad, Ali and Riahi, Pari and DeWitt, Erica and Thurber, Fey and Mahyar, Narges

evidence.rationale: Full-text evidence added in the expanded reviewed tranche.

finding.author_claim: AI interviewing was viable and broadly comparable to human interviewing, with different implementation failures.
finding.evidence_statement: Human coding found broadly similar response quality and overall guideline adherence; the AI more often missed follow-up opportunities or gave evaluative encouragement, while humans more often missed active listening or suggested answers.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Comparable averages conceal substantively different failure modes, and the small student sample makes the result proof-of-concept evidence.
finding.measure: coded interviewer behavior and response quality

sources.author: Wuttke, Alexander and Aßenmacher, Matthias and Klamm, Christopher and Lang, Max M. and Würschinger, Quirin and Kreuter, Frauke

evidence.rationale: Full-text evidence added in the expanded reviewed tranche.

finding.author_claim: Conversational platform and style jointly reduced satisficing.
finding.evidence_statement: The chatbot produced more differentiated responses than the web survey (platform F(1,102)=9.83, p<.01), with a platform-by-style interaction (F(1,102)=14.33, p<.001); dropout and ease of use did not differ significantly.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Interface and tone interact: a chatbot label or layout alone is not the operative treatment, and structured-response differentiation is only one quality dimension.
finding.measure: response differentiation index

sources.author: Kim, Soomin and Lee, Joonhwan and Gweon, Gahgene

claims.confidence_rationale: Promising expert ratings and feasibility results are based on small, heterogeneous, or nonrandomized comparisons.

claims.statement: Evidence that AI interviews yield more or richer text should not be treated as measurement validity; validity is task-specific and requires external or independent criteria.
claims.scope: AI-assisted surveys, reflective interviews, live coding, and child-witness questioning.

evidence.rationale: The mock-event experiment used externally knowable correct and false details and found task-specific efficiency gains.

finding.author_claim: LLM-formulated interviews elicited information more efficiently and with less false information than naive human interviewers.
finding.evidence_statement: LLM interviews elicited similar unique correct details (8.50 vs 7.50, p=.290), more unique correct information per question (0.90 vs 0.46, p<.001), and less false information overall, while asking 471 questions versus 872 in the human condition.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: This is unusually direct validity evidence, but it evaluates LLM-formulated questions read by a human and compares against naive—not trained forensic—interviewers.
finding.measure: blind-coded unique correct details, false details, and information per question

study.label: Sun et al. child witness interview experiment
study.design: randomized comparison of LLM-formulated and naive-human-formulated interview questions
study.setting: online interview after viewing a witnessed mock-event video
study.intervention: real-time ChatGPT-3.5 question formulation, delivered by a human assistant
study.comparator: questions formulated and delivered by naive university-student interviewers
methods: blind content coding with inter-rater reliability

appraisal.framework: review-specific mixed-method risk-of-bias and applicability appraisal

dimensions.name: internal validity
dimensions.rationale: Children were randomly assigned and answers were reliability-coded, but scheduling mechanics implemented assignment and human assistants delivered LLM questions.

dimensions.name: measurement validity
dimensions.rationale: Mock-event videos provide externally knowable correct and false details.

dimensions.name: external validity
dimensions.rationale: Young Mandarin-speaking children, naive human comparators, and a forensic mock-event constrain generalization.

appraisal.applicability: Strong evidence about question formulation and objective recall; indirect for autonomous adult qualitative interviewing.

sources.title: Comparing the Performance of a Large Language Model and Naive Human Interviewers in Interviewing Children about a Witnessed Mock-Event
sources.author: Sun, Yongjie and Pang, Haohai and Järvilehto, Liisa and Zhang, Ophelia and Shapiro, David and Korkman, Julia and Haginoya, Shumpei and Santtila, Pekka

evidence.rationale: Live-coding accuracy varied by task and respondent confirmation was contaminated by acquiescence.

finding.author_claim: Off-the-shelf live coding performed moderately well but produced inflated false positives.
finding.evidence_statement: Respondent-confirmed accuracy ranged from 66.1% to 96.2% across tasks; agreement with independent human coding was lower for several tasks, and respondents selected 'none of the above' less often.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: Live coding is task-dependent and respondent confirmation is not a neutral gold standard because the confirmation interaction itself can induce acquiescence.
finding.measure: accuracy, precision, and recall against respondent confirmation and human coding

study.population: U.S. adults recruited from a proprietary non-probability panel and quota-sampled on age, gender, and education
study.setting: Inca web conversational survey, fielded July 15-17, 2024
study.intervention: LLM-generated confirmation probes or elaboration/relevance probes, with live zero-shot coding

blind human coding of response-quality criteria

dimensions.name: internal validity

dimensions.name: measurement validity
dimensions.rationale: Multiple quality measures and human coders are strengths, but respondent confirmations are vulnerable to acquiescence and several text metrics are indirect proxies for information quality.

appraisal.applicability: Directly applicable to LLM-assisted web survey interviewing; less direct for long-form qualitative or clinical interviews.

evidence.rationale: Longer and more specific answers did not consistently contain more distributionally novel information.

finding.author_claim: Elaboration and relevance probes improved some dimensions of response quality but not others.
finding.evidence_statement: Probing increased specificity and explanation for the two opinion questions and increased word count and Shannon entropy, but did not improve completeness, relevance, lexical diversity, or KL divergence consistently.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: The experiment supports a selective enrichment effect—more detail and explanation—not a general improvement in informational novelty or every quality dimension.
finding.measure: blind qualitative coding and textual information measures

evidence.rationale: Randomized reflective interviews improved self-reported clarity, which is valuable but not external truth validation.

finding.author_claim: AI-led interviewing improved respondents' clarity and produced richer material than open-text questions.
finding.evidence_statement: In the randomized meaning-in-life study, 51.69% of AI-interview respondents said they could clearly pinpoint sources of meaning versus 41.18% in open text; 33.82% versus 41.57% said their thoughts were still evolving.
finding.reviewer_interpretation: The comparison supports a reflective effect of the interview, although self-reported clarity is not an external validation of answer truth or qualitative depth.
finding.outcome: clarity of thought about meaning in life
finding.measure: respondent self-assessment

finding.reviewer_interpretation: Conversational fluency and conventional response-quality scores can coexist with weak qualitative richness, directly qualifying general claims about adaptive probing.

article.title: Interviewing at the Marginal Cost of Computation
article.subtitle: What AI Interviewers Change About Disclosure, Adaptivity, and Measurement
article.audience: Economists, survey methodologists, and social scientists considering AI-mediated interviews
article.abstract: Adaptive interviewing has traditionally exchanged standardization and scale for interviewer judgment and conversational depth. AI interviewers relax that production constraint, but their value depends on whether conversational gains become valid measurements rather than merely longer transcripts. This review connects research on virtual humans, conversational surveys, adaptive probing, and criterion-based interview evaluation. Across seventeen papers, the evidence supports a conditional conclusion: automation can reduce evaluation apprehension and can improve selected dimensions of probing and transcript quality, yet effects depend on disclosure, trust, probe purpose, modality, and the availability of external validity criteria. The field has advanced faster on scalable elicitation than on measurement theory. Its central agenda is therefore to identify which interviewer decisions should be automated, for whom, and against which substantive benchmark.
motivation: Interviews produce contextual and open-ended evidence that fixed questionnaires often miss, but trained interviewer time makes adaptive interviewing expensive and difficult to standardize.
Large language models make contingent follow-up questions cheap to produce at scale, potentially changing the feasible frontier between standardized measurement and conversational depth.
The resulting policy and research value depends on measurement, not fluency: longer or more natural conversations need not be more accurate, comparable, or decision-relevant.
field_context: Interview design has long managed a tension between standardization, which supports comparability, and interviewer discretion, which supports clarification, rapport, and discovery.
Earlier virtual-human systems separated the social effects of perceived automation from the capabilities of generative language models; contemporary systems combine those channels.
The literature spans human-computer interaction, survey methodology, forensic interviewing, and applied economics, with different outcome standards and weak cross-field integration.
article.central_question: When does AI-mediated adaptivity improve the economic production of interview evidence, and when does it merely change respondent behavior or transcript volume without improving measurement?
article.thesis: AI interviewers relax the cost and standardization constraints on adaptive interviewing, but they do not remove the core measurement problem: benefits are conditional on respondent trust, the purpose and timing of probes, and validation against outcomes beyond transcript length or user preference.
contribution: Recasts AI interviewing as a change in the production technology of measurement rather than as a contest between humans and machines.
Connects the disclosure mechanism identified in virtual-human research to modern evidence on adaptive probing and interview quality.
Separates conversational output, respondent experience, and criterion validity, which the emerging literature often treats as interchangeable indicators of success.
Develops a research agenda centered on task allocation, heterogeneous effects, and external validation.
scope_includes: Empirical studies in which an automated conversational system conducts or materially adapts an interview or open-ended survey interaction.
Evidence on disclosure, rapport, probing behavior, respondent burden, transcript quality, factual accuracy, and comparisons with human or conventional modes.
Foundational virtual-human studies needed to identify mechanisms as well as recent generative-AI evaluations.
scope_excludes: AI used only to code or summarize interviews conducted by humans.
Generic customer-service chatbots without a data-elicitation objective.
Claims about population representativeness, downstream causal inference, or truthful reporting that the included designs do not directly test.

literatures.label: Virtual humans and disclosure
literatures.description: Early embodied-agent studies ask how perceived automation, social presence, and evaluation apprehension change what respondents reveal.
literatures.relationship_to_review: Provides the behavioral mechanism behind potential disclosure gains and distinguishes automation effects from language-model capability.

literatures.label: Conversational surveys and adaptive probes
literatures.description: Survey and HCI studies evaluate whether conversational interfaces and theoretically motivated probes improve open-ended answers and respondent experience.
literatures.relationship_to_review: Identifies design margins and shows that adaptivity has selective benefits and measurable burden costs.

literatures.label: Qualitative evidence at scale
literatures.description: Recent economics work treats AI-led conversation as infrastructure for producing rich qualitative data at survey-like scale.
literatures.relationship_to_review: Shows the frontier application and motivates the production-technology framing.

literatures.label: Criterion-based interview validity
literatures.description: Forensic-style experiments compare elicited accounts against events known to the researcher rather than treating verbosity as quality.
literatures.relationship_to_review: Supplies the strongest warning against equating more conversational output with better measurement.

source_positions.contribution: Establishes the virtual-human system lineage and feasibility of semi-automated sensitive interviewing.
source_positions.caveat: A specialized multimodal system, not a modern autonomous language-model interviewer.

source_positions.contribution: Isolates perceived automation and evaluation apprehension as mechanisms affecting disclosure.
source_positions.caveat: Disclosure willingness is not equivalent to factual accuracy or population-level validity.

source_positions.contribution: Connects embodied virtual humans to accessible survey chatbots and foregrounds user experience and trust.
source_positions.caveat: Small and context-specific evaluation with limited causal leverage.

source_positions.contribution: Provides a broad contemporary experiment on conversational interviewing, data quality, and respondent experience.
source_positions.caveat: Online tasks and study-specific quality measures bound generalization to field interviews.

source_positions.contribution: Decomposes adaptive interviewing into theory-based probe types rather than evaluating a monolithic chatbot treatment.
source_positions.caveat: Probe effects depend on question and stage; no universal optimal probe follows.

source_positions.contribution: Evaluates factual interview performance against a witnessed event and demonstrates the importance of criterion validity.
source_positions.caveat: A child-witness mock event is unusually structured and high stakes.

source_positions.contribution: Shows how AI-led interviews can scale qualitative elicitation and benchmark transcript quality against trained humans.
source_positions.caveat: Transcript-quality benchmarks do not by themselves establish construct or predictive validity.

source_positions.contribution: Demonstrates respondent-specific LLM probing in an applied market-research system.
source_positions.caveat: Parallel samples, bundled systems, and proprietary ratings limit causal and independent-validity claims.

timeline.label: Virtual-human interviewing separates automation from human evaluation
timeline.significance: The first wave establishes feasibility and a disclosure mechanism before general-purpose generative models.

timeline.label: Conversational survey chatbots move into ordinary data collection
timeline.significance: The interface becomes cheaper and more familiar, shifting attention toward usability and trust.

timeline.label: Language models begin generating respondent-specific probes
timeline.significance: Applied systems make the content and policy of follow-up questions a central design margin.

timeline.label: Generative systems enable randomized tests of adaptivity and probe design
timeline.significance: Studies begin to compare conversational treatments, isolate probe types, and test performance against external criteria.

timeline.label: AI-led interviews become infrastructure for qualitative evidence at scale
timeline.significance: The research question shifts from technical feasibility to optimal deployment and measurement validity.

sections.heading: Introduction: Interviewing as a Production Technology
sections.purpose: Begin with the economics of producing adaptive evidence, state the thesis, define scope, and preview the article.

sections.heading: From Virtual Humans to Generative Interviewers
sections.purpose: Trace the intellectual lineage and distinguish the behavioral effect of automation from advances in conversational capability.

sections.heading: What Adaptivity Produces
sections.purpose: Evaluate whether adaptive probes improve answer content, where they work, and what burden they impose.

sections.heading: Humans, Machines, and the Quality Frontier
sections.purpose: Synthesize comparative performance without collapsing different modalities, tasks, and notions of quality into a single ranking.

sections.heading: The Measurement Problem
sections.purpose: Separate disclosure, verbosity, transcript ratings, and respondent experience from criterion and construct validity.

sections.heading: An Economics Research Agenda
sections.purpose: Frame open questions as optimal task allocation, heterogeneous treatment effects, equilibrium respondent adaptation, validation, and total data-production cost.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.purpose: Return to the conditional thesis and identify what evidence would change it.

conclusion: AI changes the feasible set of interview designs by making standardized adaptivity inexpensive, not by making interviewer judgment or measurement error disappear.
The most defensible current result is conditional: automation can improve disclosure and selected forms of probing, while trust, burden, task, and modality determine whether those gains survive.

The next generation of studies should pre-specify the measurement target, benchmark against external criteria, report heterogeneous effects, and compare total production costs rather than transcript volume alone.
